item.title: China's Chang'e-6 lunar sample finds home at UN in Vienna
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-15
For Aarti Holla-Maini, director of the UN Office for Outer Space Affairs, the significance of the sample goes beyond its scientific value. "Lunar samples from the far side are so rare, but this one, thanks to China, belongs to everyone. It belongs to us all," she said. VIENNA, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- China on Monday formally presented a lunar sample collected from the far side of the Moon by its Chang'e-6 mission to the United Nations (UN) in Vienna, where the sample will be permanently exhibited. The ceremony, themed "From lunar ground to common ground: a shared future for all," brought together diplomats, UN officials, scientists and representatives of international organizations. Carried more than 380,000 km from the Moon to Earth and then to the heart of international diplomacy, the sample is more than a fragment of lunar soil and rock. It has become a symbol of scientific achievement, international cooperation and humanity's shared future in space. At the venue, the lunar sample attracted considerable attention, with diplomats, delegates and officials from international organizations stopping for a close look. Some visitors even lined up to take photographs with material retrieved from the Moon's far side. The sample has an extraordinary provenance. In 2024, China's Chang'e-6 lunar exploration mission successfully collected 1,935.3 grams of samples from the South Pole-Aitken (SPA) Basin on the far side of the Moon, marking the first time in human history that samples had been retrieved from the lunar far side. The achievement opened a new chapter in lunar science, offering scientists an unprecedented opportunity to study material from a region that has long remained beyond direct view from Earth. "It is a great honor for me to attend this ceremony today," said Austrian sinologist Richard Trappl. "Although the Moon is 380,000 kilometers away from Earth, today it has come to Vienna -- to the United Nations in Vienna -- and I extend my sincere congratulations to China." Harvey Dzodin, senior fellow of the Center for China and Globalization, said the sample's uniqueness lies in its origin. "I think it's the first time for most people to see the lunar sample from the far side of the Moon," he said. In his view, the sample can also serve as an "ambassador" for China by demonstrating the country's technological capabilities. "Obviously, the UN is the first place where the sample should be shared outside of China, because the UN is an ideal that needs to be realized. And it represents every nation," he said, expressing hope that more lunar samples can be collected and shared in the future. Aarti Holla-Maini, director of the UN Office for Outer Space Affairs, described Chang'e-6 as one of an "impressive series of unprecedented achievements" on and around the Moon in recent years. "The coming years are full of promise of yet more impressive missions," she said, adding that she looked forward to seeing what China's Chang'e-7 and Chang'e-8 missions might bring as well. For Holla-Maini, the significance of the sample goes beyond its scientific value. "Lunar samples from the far side are so rare, but this one, thanks to China, belongs to everyone. It belongs to us all," she said. She also acknowledged China's lunar sample program, through which the country has been sharing these unique resources with scientific and research institutions around the world, enabling scientists without direct access to such capabilities to benefit from them. The permanent exhibition of the sample in Vienna gives it a new role. It will no longer be confined to laboratories or specialized facilities, but will be placed in a setting visited every year by thousands of students, delegates and visitors from every corner of the world. "I'm very proud that this gift will sit here in Vienna, not as a trophy, but as a teacher," Holla-Maini said. "For us, we are all people who otherwise would never get the chance to stand so close to the Moon," Holla-Maini said. "From lunar ground to common ground, I hope that every visitor who stops in front of this rock leaves with a sense of wonder at what humanity as individuals but also collectively together can achieve." ■

item.title: Economic Watch: Reliable mainland market for Taiwan fruits challenges DPP's push for cross-Strait economic decoupling
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-15
This photo taken with a mobile phone on Sept. 9, 2026 shows pomelos at a pomelos garden in Juisui Township of Hualien County, southeast China's Taiwan. (Xinhua/Ma Xinran) TAIPEI/BEIJING, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- When fruit harvests peak, Taiwan farmers not only need favorable weather but also buyers capable of absorbing large volumes quickly. For an increasing number of them, these buyers are on the Chinese mainland, with its proximity, vast consumer market and measures to facilitate agricultural trade. In Juisui Township of east Taiwan's Hualien County, farmers are racing to harvest and pack pomelos, a seasonal fruit with a mildly sour and sweet aftertaste. For growers like Yang Ju-huang, who cultivates more than 10,000 pomelo trees across a 22-mu (about 1.47 hectares) orchard, securing sales channels is as important as producing a good crop. The pomelos grown in Juisui have relatively thick peels and can undergo a post-harvest process in which moisture gradually moves from the peel back into the flesh, making them well suited to long-distance transportation. "That gives our pomelos a particular advantage in reaching consumers across the Taiwan Strait," Yang said. Access to the mainland market has expanded this year. On Aug. 25 and Sept. 1 respectively, mainland authorities added more Taiwan pomelo orchards and packing facilities to the list eligible to export to the mainland. The Farmers' Association in Juisui said that exports to the mainland and Hong Kong Special Administrative Region are expected to further grow this year. For farmers, the significance lies not only in individual orders, but also in the predictability of demand. "Pomelos exported to the mainland have stable sales, which gives farmers greater peace of mind," said Chen Ting, a Hualien grower. This demand is increasingly visible beyond the orchards. Hualien pomelos have been showcased at major trade and agricultural events in Beijing, south China's Dongguan and Nanjing in east China this season, giving producers direct access to consumers and distributors in mainland cities. "The good harvest this year coincided with sluggish sales of some fruits in the local market, making mainland demand particularly valuable," said Tsai Yao-cheng, director of Taiwan Farmers' Association Development Co., Ltd. "Taiwan pomelos are now arriving in Nanjing every week, while Guangdong in south China and east China's Fujian are also actively seeking to introduce Taiwan fruits." The same market dynamic is even more pronounced for pineapple custard apples, one of Taitung's signature agricultural products. Pineapple custard apple orchards stretch for more than 100 km across the county. Roughly 95 percent of the island's overseas shipments of the fruit have gone to the mainland, making this market a key part of the industry's sales structure. Lin Chao-hung, head of a fruit growers' cooperative group in Beinan Township, Taitung, told Xinhua that her group established a stable partnership with a mainland warehouse retailer two years ago, enabling the fruit to reach mainland shelves from the orchard in as little as nine days. The mainland has traditionally been a major market for Taiwan farm produce. In 2019, the mainland was the largest export market for such produce, taking up a share of 22.9 percent of the island's total farm produce exports. However, driven by a cross-Strait economic decoupling policy, Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities intentionally abandoned the mainland market that is geographically close, connected by relatively short shipping routes, and capable of absorbing large volumes of seasonal produce. Meanwhile, the mainland has never stopped trying to reconnect and promote agricultural exchanges across the Strait. The mainland in April rolled out a package of 10 policies and measures to promote cross-Strait exchanges and cooperation. One of these measures aims to facilitate the entry of Taiwan agricultural and fishery products that meet quarantine requirements and supports their participation in mainland trade fairs to expand sales channels. Implementation has since moved beyond policy announcements to concrete trade facilitation. At the Straits Forum in June, a matchmaking and signing event brought together Taiwan agricultural and fishery producers and mainland buyers. Mainland companies signed procurement agreements with enterprises and industry associations from several Taiwan localities covering products ranging from pineapple custard apples to pomelos and tea. Figures point to a broader trend. According to Taiwan's agricultural authorities, the island's total agricultural exports declined in the first half of 2026, as shipments to the United States and Japan fell. By contrast, exports to the mainland rose 11.3 percent in this period, with pineapple custard apples among the main growth items. Yet the expansion of agricultural trade has not been matched by an equally open and facilitating approach from Taiwan authorities. When mainland enterprises placed orders for Taiwan agricultural and fishery products, including pineapple custard apples from Taitung and groupers from Pingtung, at the Straits Forum matchmaking event, the DPP authorities accused the mainland of using agricultural products as a political tool and launched investigations into five Taiwan agricultural and fishery organizations that participated in the event. This episode underscored the gap between the commercial nature of cross-Strait agricultural exchanges and the political lens through which they are viewed by the DPP authorities. A similar pattern has emerged in tourism and other areas covered by the 10 measures. While the mainland has sought to promote people-to-people exchanges and expand business links, the DPP authorities have imposed additional political conditions and administrative barriers on such contacts. "The 10 measures fully align with the common interests of people on both sides of the Strait," said Sheng Jiuyuan, director of the center for Taiwan studies at Shanghai Jiao Tong University in east China. These measures, he said, are pragmatic steps to promote the peaceful development of cross-Strait relations and deepen integrated development, with benefits reaching grassroots farmers and fishermen, small and micro businesses, young people and other groups in Taiwan. After the measures were released, the DPP authorities immediately launched a campaign to discredit them, Sheng said, arguing that such efforts deliberately fueled confrontation across the Strait and played up the so-called "mainland threat" to divert attention from governance problems. "The DPP authorities' actions were driven entirely by the party's own political interests at the expense of the island's overall development and the well-being and livelihoods of its people," Sheng noted. For Taiwan's fruit growers, however, the calculation is more straightforward: when harvests arrive, a reliable market matters. For an increasing number of them, the mainland remains a market large enough, close enough and stable enough to make a tangible difference. "A sufficient and stable market is the most practical guarantee," Lin Chao-hung from Taitung said. ■ This photo taken with a mobile phone on Sept. 9, 2026 shows workers packing pomelos at a pomelos delivery station in Hualien County, southeast China's Taiwan. (Xinhua/Ma Xinran) This photo taken on Sept. 9, 2026 shows pomelos at a pomelos garden in Juisui Township of Hualien County, southeast China's Taiwan. (Xinhua/Huang Yang)

item.title: Xinhua Headlines: 30 years of partnership narrows China's regional divide
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-15
* In 1996, China launched a pairing initiative linking coastal Fujian Province with landlocked Ningxia as part of the country's east-west poverty alleviation collaboration program. * The east-west collaboration program is part of a broader national strategy to narrow regional development gaps and promote common prosperity. * Through this model, the country has formed an all-round pattern of poverty alleviation and targeted support at various levels, providing a "Chinese solution" for countries around the world to address poverty. YINCHUAN, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- A lifelong farmer from northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, Wang Guozhong has taken on a new role at the age of 64 by stepping onto the stage as an actor. He now stars as the lead in a play at "See Minning Drama Village," China's first theater complex themed around the country's fight against poverty. Located in Minning Town in Ningxia's Yongning County, the complex stages more than 100 performances a day, featuring 36 original productions. Many of the plays are inspired by Minning's history of resettlement and development, with performers like Wang bringing their firsthand experiences to the stage. "When we cry on stage, it is because we really went hungry back then. When we laugh, it is because we are now living a life we once could only dream of," he said. Wang was born in Xihaigu, a place the United Nations deemed the "most unfit place for human settlement" in the 1970s due to severe drought and ecological fragility. Three decades ago, China launched a pairing initiative linking coastal Fujian Province with landlocked Ningxia to target poverty alleviation as part of the country's east-west poverty alleviation collaboration program. At the time, Fujian's GDP stood at 260 billion yuan (about 38 billion U.S. dollars), dwarfing Ningxia's 20.29 billion yuan to roughly one-thirteenth. In 1997, construction began on Minning Village on barren land near Yinchuan, the regional capital. The cross-provincial effort transformed Minning, named after the abbreviations of Fujian and Ningxia, into a modern town, with a population rising from some 8,000 to over 60,000, mainly living on growing wine grapes, mushrooms, and goji berries and raising cattle. The theater complex has become another source of employment. Since its opening in July, it has helped create jobs and boost incomes for around 2,500 local residents. "For me, earning 4,000 yuan a month means I can have a stable income without leaving home," Wang said. "More importantly, I can tell our story to audiences and let more people know how east-west collaboration has changed ordinary people's lives." Wang's personal transformation mirrors a broader historical shift. Figures show that the east-west collaboration has helped Ningxia eradicate absolute poverty, lifting 803,000 rural residents out of destitution. Since 1996, Fujian has channeled 7.68 billion yuan in aid, guided over 1,600 enterprises to invest in Ningxia, with actual invested funds exceeding 100 billion yuan. Today, nearly 6,000 Fujian-based enterprises operate steadily in Ningxia, laying a solid foundation for the region's socioeconomic development, according to Wang Jian, head of Ningxia's regional department of agriculture and rural affairs. In 2025, Ningxia's per capita GDP reached 78,000 yuan, nearly 19 times higher than in 1996, underlining a compelling story of success. Guided increasingly by market forces, the two regions are facilitating a two-way flow of resources. Their digital cooperation stands out as a prime example, as Ningxia's computing resources are meeting Fujian's rising demand while helping to ease Fujian's energy constraints. This synergy is not only transforming Ningxia's resource advantages into new economic drivers but also establishing a new model for east-west digital cooperation. China's east-west collaboration program is part of a broader national strategy to narrow regional development gaps and promote common prosperity. Over years of experimentation, the program has developed a relatively mature system featuring joint coordination, paired assistance, financial support, exchanges of officials and professionals, and broad participation from businesses and society. By combining capital and markets from the east with resources from the west, the initiative has helped spark thriving local industries. For instance, the partnership between the eastern Jiangsu and northwestern Shaanxi transformed Ankang, a city in Shaanxi Province, into a "plush toy capital," with over 800 enterprises generating an annual output of 10 billion yuan and employing nearly 20,000 people. Similarly, the economic powerhouse of Guangdong and the less developed Guizhou in southwest China created a "guitar capital" in Guizhou's Zheng'an County through a cross-regional model linking Macao's design, manufacturing in Zheng'an and sales in Guangdong's Hengqin, boosting exports to 248 million yuan in 2025. Furthermore, agricultural trade has evolved from emergency charity sales to stable market integration, with Shanghai now hosting over 300 direct outlets for Yunnan's specialty products. As a long-term institutional arrangement for promoting coordinated regional development and common prosperity, the east-west collaboration has been upgraded from phased poverty alleviation measures to long-term and stable cooperation mechanisms. China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) released this year underscores the need to optimize the east-west collaboration. As 2026 marks the first year of implementing regular assistance, Chinese leadership urges drawing on the valuable experience gained from the Fujian-Ningxia partnership to further refine these mechanisms and broaden the scope of cooperation. Maierdan Mugaiti, vice minister of agriculture and rural affairs, said China would maintain the long-term pairing of eight eastern provincial-level areas with 10 western ones. Additionally, economically developed eastern counties will be linked with key western counties for rural revitalization, ensuring paired assistance reaches a wide range of people. Through this model, the country has formed an all-round pattern of poverty alleviation and targeted support at various levels, providing a "Chinese solution" for countries around the world to address poverty. In July, officials, experts and scholars from more than 50 countries visited Ningxia to decode Chinese modernization by exploring and learning from local poverty alleviation stories. Ghulom Halimzoda, chairman of the Socialist Party of Tajikistan, valued most from the Ningxia trip a complete set of institutions and mechanisms for socioeconomic operation, which could be borrowed by Central Asian countries. "The core inspiration China's experience brings us is not simply that huge resources were invested. The continuity of policy, the governance capacity to coordinate and mobilize all forces, and, most crucially, the people-centered principle are what matter most," he said. (Video reporter: Lyu Ze; Video editors: Hong Ling and Li Qin) ■

item.title: China's economy sustains momentum as new growth drivers strengthen
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-15
BEIJING, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- China's economy maintained steady momentum boosted by innovation-led and high-quality development in August, with production and supply growing steadily, employment and prices generally stable, and foreign trade registering rapid growth, official data showed on Tuesday. Fu Linghui, a spokesperson for the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS), said the economy in August showed fast growth in emerging industries. In August, the value added of industrial enterprises above the designated size grew 5.2 percent year on year, up 0.7 percentage points from the previous month, NBS data showed. Value added in equipment manufacturing rose 12.1 percent, and that in high-tech manufacturing jumped 16.7 percent, 6.9 percentage points and 11.5 percentage points faster than the industrial sector as a whole. In August, lithium-ion battery and industrial robot output expanded 57.2 percent and 34.6 percent year on year, respectively. The output of 3D printing equipment rose 29.9 percent year-on-year. New growth drivers contributed over 60 percent to growth in industrial output above the designated size in August, while information transmission, software and information technology services contributed more than 20 percent to growth in the services production index, according to Fu. The services sector grew steadily, with the services production index up 4.1 percent year on year in August. Information transmission, software and information technology services rose 9.6 percent, leasing and business services 9 percent, and transport, storage and postal services 4.8 percent. Market sales rose, with retail services growing fast. In the first eight months, the total retail sales of goods and services rose 2.5 percent year on year, with services up 4.9 percent and goods up 1.0 percent. Fixed-asset investment declined in the first eight months, down 7.2 percent year on year to around 29.3 trillion yuan, yet its structure kept improving. Wang Guanhua, another NBS spokesperson, attributed the decline to several factors, including frequent extreme weather such as high temperatures, typhoons, and floods; a complex and volatile external environment; and cautious corporate investment decisions amid the ongoing transition from old growth drivers to new ones. "What matters more is whether the investment is effective, whether it is directed to transformation and upgrading, and whether it can build momentum for long-term development," Wang said. Investment in high-tech industries grew 5.2 percent and spending on equipment 9.3 percent in the first eight months, NBS data showed, while investment in internet-related and other services under the "six networks" initiative surged 42 percent. Imports and exports of goods grew fast and the trade structure continued to optimize. In August, total goods trade reached 4.65 trillion yuan, up 19.8 percent year on year, with exports up 18.6 percent to 2.73 trillion yuan and imports up 21.7 percent to 1.92 trillion yuan. In the first eight months, total foreign trade rose 17.6 percent to 34.78 trillion yuan, with exports of mechanical and electrical products up 21.9 percent. Employment remained generally stable. The urban surveyed unemployment rate averaged 5.2 percent in the first eight months. In August, the rate stood at 5.3 percent, up 0.1 percentage points from the previous month, mainly due to the seasonal impact of new graduates entering the labor market, Fu said. Consumer prices rose mildly while producer prices grew faster year on year. In August, the consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.8 percent year on year, up 0.3 percentage points from the previous month, and the producer price index (PPI) for industrial products rose 3.8 percent, also up 0.3 percentage points. China's property market showed signs of stabilization. Total property transaction volume improved. The floor space of newly built commercial housing sold from January to August fell 12.1 percent year on year, while second-hand housing transactions rose 10.6 percent. "Despite fewer new-home transactions, the overall transaction volume of the property market has stabilized with more second-hand housing deals," Fu said. The year-on-year decline in housing prices narrowed, with new-home prices in 38 of the 70 major cities falling less than the previous month, and second-hand home prices in 48 cities falling less than the previous month. New commercial housing inventory continued to fall, with unsold floor space down 1.1 percent year on year by the end of August, the sixth consecutive monthly decline. Looking ahead, Fu said that amid a complex international environment and pressures from domestic transformation, China will step up counter-cyclical adjustment, expand domestic demand, optimize supply, deepen reform and opening up, and boost momentum and vitality to promote sustained innovation-driven, high-quality, and sound economic development. ■

item.title: Xi Story: Making canals channels for connectivity, prosperity, better life
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-15
NANNING, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- Sitting in a glass case at a museum in south China's Qinzhou, a glazed porcelain bowl etched with a floral pattern offers a tantalizing clue to this coastal city's maritime-trade past. Despite being centuries old, the bowl bears scarcely any signs of use. Experts believe that the bowl, instead of being made for use in local households, was likely among the merchandise stockpiled for trade during the Song Dynasty (960-1279), when sugar and ceramics were shipped from Qinzhou to Southeast Asian countries along the Maritime Silk Road. A historic port city on the coast of the Beibu Gulf in the South China Sea, Qinzhou, located in Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, is gaining fresh momentum as a maritime hub with the opening of the Pinglu Canal, a major river-to-sea canal project set to become operational on Wednesday. The canal stretches along the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor, a strategic trade route connecting China's inland regions with ASEAN and other global markets. During an inspection tour of Guangxi in December 2023, Chinese President Xi Jinping was briefed on the construction progress of the canal in front of a sand-table model. Guangxi's future growth potential lies in connecting its waterways to the sea and realizing integrated river-sea transport, Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, said during that trip. He added that Guangxi should strengthen itself via maritime development, noting that the region has both a strong need and great potential to further expand opening up, both internally and externally. Running from north to south, the Pinglu Canal links the Xijiang River shipping route with the Beibu Gulf. It is expected to shorten the shipping distance between China's southwestern hinterland and ASEAN, China's largest trading partner, by 560 km and reduce logistics costs by 18 to 30 percent, according to Lu Xinning, vice chairperson of the regional government of Guangxi. China's natural river systems generally run from west to east toward the sea, making it difficult to rely on existing rivers and lakes to connect the country's north and south. China has a long history of building canals. The best-known is the more than 2,500-year-old Grand Canal, the world's oldest and longest artificial waterway system, and a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2014. Xi has attached great importance to the protection and revitalization of the Grand Canal. He once stressed that the Grand Canal is a "precious heritage passed down to us by our ancestors." In 2006, when he was secretary of the CPC Zhejiang Provincial Committee, he took a "water bus" along a section of the Grand Canal in the provincial capital Hangzhou to inspect cleanup and revitalization of the canal. The "water bus" passenger service, launched in 2004, was the first of its kind along an urban Grand Canal network. Along the way, Xi asked in detail about everything from waterway network protection and shipping operations to the development of scenic areas along the canal. He encouraged Hangzhou officials to turn the canal into "a canal for the people" and "a canal for visitors," stressing that the people should be the ultimate beneficiaries. His attention to the Grand Canal has remained unchanged over the years. In November 2020, as China's top leader, Xi visited the eastern city of Yangzhou, where some of the waterway system's oldest sections are located. "For centuries, the canal has nourished the cities and people along its banks, bringing prosperity and well-being to them," he said. "I hope everyone will work together to protect the Grand Canal and ensure that it continues to benefit the people for generations to come," he told local officials and residents. Yangzhou, described by Xi as a "wonderful place built along the water, thriving on it and made beautiful by it," is a vivid example of how the Grand Canal has nourished a city and shaped its fortunes. Just like Yangzhou, Qinzhou today is poised to reap the benefits of greater connectivity -- this time, connectivity from river to sea, thanks to the Pinglu Canal. The Pinglu Canal is bringing to life the historical tradition of the Grand Canal in a new era, a tradition of fostering prosperity through waterways, said Xie Zhujun, a researcher with the Guangxi Academy of Social Sciences. Ultimately, the purpose of a canal is to improve people's livelihoods and deliver broader economic and social benefits, he noted. For Ning Qiongri, a Qinzhou native and a vlogger who has posted some 1,600 videos chronicling the construction of the Pinglu Canal, the project promises not only greater prosperity, but also a better life for local people. "Many people find jobs thanks to the canal's construction. I've also seen brand-new villages and schools built along its banks, as well as supermarkets and restaurants that are eager to name themselves after the canal," Ning revealed. ■

item.title: Xinhua Commentary: Stronger BRICS cooperation for greater Global South development
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-15
BEIJING, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- For BRICS, solid practical cooperation among its 11 member countries and 10 partner countries is essential to deliver more concrete gains and meaningful progress. That was a key message delivered by Chinese President Xi Jinping at the recent 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi. Beginning in 2006 with four members, the mechanism has become the world's most influential platform for cooperation among emerging markets and developing countries. BRICS countries must seize the historical initiative, rally the Global South, be an active, stabilizing and positive force in international affairs, and advance the well-being of all humanity, Xi urged. Since its inception, the BRICS mechanism has been closely linked with the aspirations of emerging markets and developing countries. The members now have both the capacity and responsibility to amplify their common voice in international affairs and work with fellow developing countries toward common prosperity. As BRICS cooperation enters a new stage of development, the task is clear: to make it broader, deeper and more effective. In New Delhi, Xi put forward five initiatives aimed precisely at that goal: the open source and inclusive artificial intelligence (AI) initiative, the trade and investment facilitation initiative, the digital industry cooperation initiative, the intelligent manufacturing cooperation initiative, and the science and technology talent development initiative. These proposals tackle some of the most consequential factors shaping the global economy today, with technological innovation as a common thread. A new round of scientific and technological revolution and industrial transformation, epitomized by the rapid development of AI, is reshaping the pattern of global development. Leveraging AI for economic growth and social good would be essential for promoting a just, fair, equitable and prosperous future for all countries, especially those of the Global South. In this regard, Xi called on BRICS to become a "pioneer in advancing innovation-driven development" at the summit, pointing out the future direction of BRICS practical cooperation. More importantly, China's proposals are backed by concrete measures. China will take the lead in establishing a BRICS AI open source community, push for establishing a BRICS digital ecosystem cloud platform, and assist fellow BRICS countries in building smart factories. It also proposes a BRICS special economic zone partnership and a BRICS engineer cultivation alliance. These steps embody an enduring feature of China's approach to BRICS cooperation: turning consensus into action and proposals into tangible results. BRICS is not a talking shop, but a task force that gets things done. Its vitality comes from action, and its appeal comes from results. This year marks the beginning of China's 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030). By aligning its development with the needs of fellow BRICS countries and the broader Global South, China is injecting fresh impetus into greater BRICS cooperation and demonstrating through concrete action its commitment to common development. ■

item.title: Xi urges Chinese police to remain committed to serving people with responsibility, dedication
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-15
BEIJING, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping has called on the country's police officers to remain committed to serving the people, be loyal guardians of the Party and the people, and demonstrate a strong sense of responsibility and dedication. Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks in a reply letter to a primary-level police force from Zhangzhou, east China's Fujian Province. In his letter to the "Zhangzhou 110" police unit, Xi lauded its police officers for their dedication and hard work at the grassroots level in serving the public and maintaining social stability for the people. He emphasized that the police bear the important responsibility of safeguarding the people's well-being and the country's peace, calling on Chinese police to uphold fine traditions, devote themselves to wholeheartedly addressing the needs and concerns of the people, and work diligently to protect the safety of the public. The "Zhangzhou 110" unit is one of the exemplary primary-level units within China's police forces. Since 1990, it has pioneered and continuously improved a rapid response mechanism tied to the 110 police emergency call service, playing a significant role in combating crime, maintaining public security, and serving the community. During his tenure in Fujian, Xi visited the police unit three times to inspect and guide its work. Recently, members of the unit wrote to Xi, reporting on their work and expressing their determination to fulfill duties on the new journey. ■

item.title: Xi's article on advancing basic research to be published
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-15
BEIJING, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- An article by Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, on strengthening basic research will be published on Wednesday. The article by Xi, also Chinese president and chairman of the Central Military Commission, will be published in this year's 18th issue of the Qiushi Journal, a flagship magazine of the CPC Central Committee. Noting that basic research is the bedrock of the entire scientific system and a frontier area of global sci-tech competition, the article emphasizes further efforts to develop the country's basic research to build China into a leading country in science and technology. Compared with global leaders in science and technology, China still lags behind in basic research, the article says, calling for stronger efforts and more concrete measures to strengthen basic research, enhance the country's capacity for original innovation, and accelerate efforts toward greater self-reliance and strength in science and technology. The layout of basic research should be optimized, with the main directions and priority areas for basic research further clarified based on the country's urgent and long-term needs, the article says. It also underscores the importance of promoting coordinated development of applied disciplines and basic disciplines, while encouraging integration among different disciplines and interdisciplinary research. The article calls for efforts to expand the basic research talent pool and provide greater support for young talent. It also stresses the importance of inspiring the imagination and curiosity of young people, so that more of them will regard pursuing basic research as a lifelong aspiration. On ramping up support for basic research, the article calls for gradually raising the proportion of funding for basic research while strengthening the systematic development of major scientific and technological infrastructure. Attention should also be paid to AI-empowered basic research and the development of a system of intelligent research platforms, it adds. The article also urges the country's active integration into the global innovation network, boosting original innovation capacity through openness and cooperation. It also emphasizes the need to further open up national science and technology programs, take the lead in initiating and participating in international big science programs and projects, and take an active part in global scientific and technological governance. ■
